---
title: "Intermediate Representation and SSA — Name Every Computed Value Once"
description: "A rigorous introductory lesson with one small example, mathematical notation and a proof-oriented explanation."
---

## Start with an ordinary situation

Compilers optimise code more easily after translating it from source syntax into a smaller set of explicit operations.

## The core concept

An intermediate representation (IR) isolates operations from source-language surface syntax. Static Single Assignment (SSA) gives each defined IR value one assignment in its definition path.

## Express it mathematically

$$
v_1=2,\quad v_2=3,\quad v_3=v_1+v_2
$$

**Every symbol explained:** v1,v2,v3 are unique IR value names; '=' denotes their definitions, not a mutable variable assignment. The final operation adds two known values.

**Substitute actual numbers:** v1=2, v2=3, v3=2+3=5. The source 'x=2; y=3; z=x+y' can be expressed by the three operations. A compiler can then fold v3 to the constant 5 if no semantic constraint prevents it.

## Why it works

SSA simplifies def-use analysis. Control-flow joins use mechanisms such as phi nodes (or block arguments in different IRs) to select a value depending on the predecessor block.

## Go one level deeper

SSA does not mean a physical CPU register exists for every symbolic name. Lowering and register allocation later map values to constrained machine resources.

## Common misunderstanding

Real optimisations must preserve observable behaviour, including effects, exceptions, overflow conventions, memory ordering and undefined-behaviour rules.

## Check your understanding

Explain the example with different numbers. Identify which assumption makes the derivation work, and which assumption would invalidate it. Then write the mathematical model again without looking.
